L04.title: Relate elapsed time to flight distance
L04.objective: Pair flight positions with elapsed times and explain the change in distance over successive intervals.

L14.objective: Explain how two systems work together and why taking care of one supports the functioning of the other.

L34.title: Test how the number of bulbs affects brightness
L34.objective: Change the number of bulbs in series and parallel circuits, holding the cell supply constant. Record the effect on brightness.

L35.title: Test how the number of dry cells affects brightness
L35.objective: Change the number of dry cells and observe bulb brightness in each circuit type. Identify the factors kept constant.

L40.title: Measure temperature from ice to boiling
L40.objective: Record the temperature of water over time and use the data to identify its freezing and boiling points.

L54.objective: Model reflected sunlight and show the direction and approximate duration of the Moon's rotation and revolution.

L60.title: Propose and explain a sustainable tool
L60.objective: Label the simple machines in a tool for a daily problem and justify a feature that makes it last longer or easier to maintain.

L01.materials: Two folded paper planes, observation grid
L01.induction: Show one narrow-wing and one broad-wing plane. Ask pupils what they can see before either plane flies.
L01.teach: Model comparing the same feature on both planes. Ask groups to explain their sorting rule.
L01.practice: Describe two visible differences and regroup four planes by wing width or nose shape.
L01.assessment: Describe P and Q using the same two features. Give a rule for sorting and classify both.
L01.evidence: P has broader wings and a blunt nose. Q has narrow wings and a pointed nose. Either stated feature works as a consistent sorting rule.
L01.closure: Ask one pupil to distinguish an observation from a guess about flight.

L02.materials: Paper planes, tape measure, floor markers, results grid
L02.induction: Point out the start line and a landing marker. Ask where the zero mark belongs.
L02.teach: Demonstrate measuring straight from the start line to first contact, with zero aligned. Assign a clear flight lane.
L02.practice: Launch three times from the same line. Mark first contact and record distance in centimetres under Trial 1, 2 and 3.
L02.assessment: Submit three labelled readings and demonstrate how one reading was obtained.
L02.evidence: All readings use cm and refer to the distance from the fixed launch line to the first landing point.
L02.closure: Ask why start points and units have to agree before distances can be compared.

L03.materials: Paper planes, trial-distance cards, inference slips
L03.induction: Show a trial where a paper plane nosedives. Elicit what pupils saw and one possible explanation.
L03.teach: Compare the observed distance with a plausible reason. Ask which follow-up comparison would test the inference.
L03.practice: Compare three trials for each plane. Write an inference and a prediction for a fourth flight under the same conditions.
L03.assessment: A reaches 210, 225 and 220 cm. B reaches 105, 110 and 112 cm. Predict which will go farther in the next trial and suggest why.
L03.evidence: A is a reasonable prediction because it flew farther in all three trials. A feature such as wing shape is a possible explanation to test.
L03.closure: Ask which statement is a prediction and which is an inference.

L04.materials: Flight snapshot cards, timer, tape measure, data sheets
L04.induction: Show two pictures of the same moving plane. Ask which came first and what evidence helps.
L04.teach: Model pairing distance with elapsed time. Show why ordering snapshots by distance alone could fail if the plane turns.
L04.practice: Arrange timed snapshots. Tabulate time and distance from the start line, then describe how the distance changes.
L04.assessment: Order the given 0, 1 and 2 second cards. Interpret the paired distances 0, 120 and 200 cm. Which one-second interval adds more distance?
L04.evidence: Distance increases in both intervals. It increases by 120 cm in the first second and 80 cm in the second.
L04.closure: Ask how a timestamp helps when two photographs show similar positions.

L05.materials: Bubble solution, two labelled mixtures, matching wands, timer cards
L05.induction: Ask what observable event should stop a bubble timer.
L05.teach: Model a measurable start and end. Change only the mixture and elicit how to keep the bubble test fair.
L05.practice: Write a definition, identify variables and draft a hypothesis that can be tested by timed trials.
L05.assessment: Define bubble duration. Name the changed, measured and one controlled variable. Write an if–then hypothesis.
L05.evidence: Duration runs from detachment from the wand to bursting. Mixture changes, duration is measured in seconds, and wand size or airflow stays the same.
L05.closure: Ask pupils to point to the exact event that starts and stops the timer.

L06.materials: Two pre-mixed solutions, identical wands, protective trays, timers
L06.induction: Show one empty results grid and ask how many trials would compare two mixtures fairly.
L06.teach: Demonstrate start and stop cues. Organise groups to repeat the same test three times for each mixture without changing wands or position.
L06.practice: Time bubbles from detachment to bursting. Record all six observations, then compare the results before writing a provisional claim.
L06.assessment: Submit the six timed trials with units. Identify the variable kept constant and state what the readings suggest.
L06.evidence: The table contains three times for each mixture. The claim uses the observed results and names the controlled condition.
L06.closure: Ask how a missed timing cue could change one result.

L07.materials: Completed bubble trial sheets, report frames, comparison data
L07.induction: Display two groups' results. Ask whether a single long-lasting bubble is enough to support a claim.
L07.teach: Model linking the problem, variables, method, table and conclusion. Discuss what to report if trials disagree.
L07.practice: Write a short investigation report and swap it with a partner to check that the conclusion cites measured times.
L07.assessment: For mixture A at 6, 8 and 7 s and B at 11, 10 and 12 s, state whether the hypothesis that B lasts longer is supported.
L07.evidence: B lasts longer in every example trial. A usable report names the variables, records the timings and cites this comparison in the conclusion.
L07.closure: Ask what should be repeated if one trial contradicts the general pattern.

R01.induction: Show two plane result columns and ask which factor could have been changed.
R01.teach: Work through one practice card on keeping the launch height constant.
R01.practice: Read a fresh comparison card and annotate what changes, what is measured and what stays constant.
R01.assessment: Compare 90 and 130 cm. Name the outcome measured, a controlled factor and an evidence-based conclusion. Use the scenario card to identify what was changed.
R01.evidence: Distance is measured in cm. Start line or height can be held constant. The changed factor comes from the scenario. The second trial travelled 40 cm farther.
R01.closure: Ask one pupil to give the evidence before stating the conclusion.

L08.materials: Body outline, skeleton diagram, label cards
L08.induction: Ask pupils to touch the side of their head and locate the hard structure beneath.
L08.teach: Point out the skull, backbone, ribs and limb bones on the diagram. Model linking a structure to its function.
L08.practice: Place bone labels on outlines. Explain to a partner how one structure protects, supports or helps movement.
L08.assessment: Label the four main skeletal parts. Explain what the skull and ribs protect.
L08.evidence: Skull protects the brain, ribs protect organs such as the heart and lungs, and backbone and limb labels are correctly positioned.
L08.closure: Ask which bone structure supports the trunk.

L09.materials: Skeleton outline, joint markers, paper hinge
L09.induction: Bend the elbow and ask pupils to point to the place where the movement happens.
L09.teach: Show the elbow, knee and shoulder on a model. Compare a bend-and-straighten movement with the wider shoulder movement.
L09.practice: Mark the joints and demonstrate one movement at each location without forcing it.
L09.assessment: Label elbow and knee and describe what each joint does during bending.
L09.evidence: Each mark sits where bones meet. The elbow allows the forearm to bend, and the knee lets the lower leg bend during movement.
L09.closure: Ask how the joint in the paper hinge resembles the elbow.

L10.induction: Show a paper arm with its joint fixed. Ask what movement is lost.
L10.teach: Model using a fastener to join two bones and compare rigid support with a movable join.
L10.practice: Build and label a paper skeleton with a movable elbow or knee. Explain the need for support and protection.
L10.assessment: Show one motion in the model and explain why a skull and backbone matter in the body.
L10.evidence: The marked joint moves between labelled bones. The skull protects the brain, and the backbone helps support the body.
L10.closure: Ask which feature of the paper model represents a joint.

L11.materials: Heart and lung diagram, arrow cards, role labels
L11.induction: Ask what makes a pulse detectable after movement.
L11.teach: Trace a circuit of heart, vessels, lungs and body. Explain pumping, transport and gas exchange.
L11.practice: Place the four part cards and assign one role to each in a diagram.
L11.assessment: Label heart, vessels, lungs and blood. Write the role of each.
L11.evidence: The heart pumps, vessels carry blood, lungs exchange gases, and blood carries oxygen and other substances.
L11.closure: Ask which organ pumps blood through both pathways.

L12.materials: Heart, lungs and body cards, solid and dashed arrows
L12.induction: Show an incomplete heart–lung loop and ask where the return arrow goes.
L12.teach: Model both loops. Use arrow labels to distinguish blood richer in oxygen from blood richer in carbon dioxide.
L12.practice: Build the two loops with cards. Trace each route aloud before drawing the diagram.
L12.assessment: Draw arrows for heart–lungs–heart and heart–body–heart. Label the oxygen-rich return from the lungs and the carbon-dioxide-rich return from the body.
L12.evidence: Both loops start and return to the heart. The return from the lungs is oxygen rich and the return from the body is richer in carbon dioxide.
L12.closure: Ask why the heart appears in both loops.

L13.materials: Cell delivery cards, pathway arrows, short scenario sheet
L13.induction: Ask how oxygen from the lungs reaches a leg muscle.
L13.teach: Model a route for oxygen and for nutrients. Follow a waste example from the cells towards removal.
L13.practice: Sort delivery and removal cards. Explain how the flows support one body part.
L13.assessment: Explain why an active muscle needs circulation. Include one substance delivered and one removed.
L13.evidence: Blood brings oxygen or nutrients to muscle cells and carries carbon dioxide or other wastes away.
L13.closure: Ask learners to name one delivery and one removal in the same sentence.

L14.materials: Body-system labels, route cards, scenario pictures
L14.induction: Ask pupils where oxygen and nutrients enter the body's transport routes.
L14.teach: Connect lungs or digestive tract to nearby blood vessels. Ask how care for one system supports another.
L14.practice: Make a two-system flow chart and explain a healthy habit that supports efficient functioning.
L14.assessment: Show how the respiratory and circulatory systems work together. Explain why protecting the lungs matters to the rest of the body.
L14.evidence: Oxygen enters blood in the lungs and is carried to tissues. Healthy lungs support oxygen supply for the body.
L14.closure: Ask pupils to show which arrows cross from one system to another.

L15.materials: Habit cards, body-system mat, foldable checklist
L15.induction: Show pictures of regular activity, a balanced meal and good posture. Ask which systems each supports.
L15.teach: Model linking a habit to a clear reason and to more than one system when appropriate.
L15.practice: Design a three-item checklist. Add one labelled diagram showing how two systems contribute during an everyday activity.
L15.assessment: Submit three habits with reasons and point out two related systems in the diagram.
L15.evidence: Balanced meals supply nutrients, regular activity supports fitness, and safe posture reduces strain. Each reason connects to a named system.
L15.closure: Ask which checklist item can be practised at school.

R02.materials: Skeleton outline, body-system cards, route arrows
R02.induction: Show an elbow marker and an unlabeled lung card. Ask which systems they belong to.
R02.teach: Review one bone protection example and model the start of a blood flow diagram.
R02.practice: Use arrow cards to complete the lung pathway and add one related system.
R02.assessment: Mark the elbow, complete heart–lungs–heart and describe how the respiratory and circulatory systems work together.
R02.evidence: Elbow joins upper and lower arm. Blood goes from the heart to the lungs and back. Oxygen passes into the blood at the lungs.
R02.closure: Ask pupils to check both arrowheads on the loop.

L16.materials: Tortoise, porcupine and camouflage picture cards
L16.induction: Show the outline of a camouflaged animal and ask why it is hard to spot.
L16.teach: Distinguish the continued existence of a species from one animal's immediate escape. Link shell and spines to protection.
L16.practice: Sort physical defences and illustrate the threat reduced by each.
L16.assessment: Define survival of a species and explain why a shell and spines can help an animal survive.
L16.evidence: A species survives when successive generations continue and avoid extinction. Shell covers soft parts and spines deter attacks.
L16.closure: Ask which trait offers cover and which deters contact.

L17.materials: Lizard, squid and moth picture sequences
L17.induction: Reveal the last frame of a lizard escape sequence and ask what distracted the predator.
L17.teach: Distinguish a defensive action from a body feature. Model the chain of threat, response and escape.
L17.practice: Draw two three-frame sequences, using examples such as tail detachment or release of ink.
L17.assessment: Explain one behaviour in each of two animals and identify the threat it counters.
L17.evidence: A lizard's released tail distracts a predator. A squid's ink clouds the water and helps it escape a predator.
L17.closure: Ask pupils to locate the exact frame in which the defence helps.

L18.materials: Weather cards, animal images, comparison chart
L18.induction: Show a hot afternoon and freezing winter picture. Ask what difficulties an animal faces in each.
L18.teach: Model linking temperature or scarcity to an action, using a buffalo wallowing and a hibernating animal.
L18.practice: Make a cold versus hot comparison with one behaviour and reason in each column.
L18.assessment: Explain how wallowing helps a buffalo in hot conditions and how hibernation helps an animal in a cold season.
L18.evidence: Wallowing helps cool the buffalo. Hibernation reduces activity and energy use when conditions are cold and food is scarce.
L18.closure: Ask why the same response would not solve both weather problems.

L19.materials: Egg and nest pictures, shelter cards, role-play prompts
L19.induction: Show an exposed egg model and ask what could threaten it.
L19.teach: Compare hidden eggs with eggs kept warm by an adult. Supply examples of crocodile nesting and penguin incubation.
L19.practice: Use cards to enact one behaviour, then draw a labelled sketch linking it to egg survival.
L19.assessment: Explain how hiding a nest and keeping an egg warm solve different risks.
L19.evidence: Covering a nest can reduce detection. Incubation helps maintain a suitable temperature for development.
L19.closure: Ask which protective action addresses a change in temperature.

L20.materials: Kangaroo, crocodile and hen photo cards, folded chart
L20.induction: Ask which dangers a young animal encounters when it first leaves its shelter.
L20.teach: Model comparing two ways parents protect young, noting what each behaviour protects against.
L20.practice: Use a folded chart to compare one shelter behaviour and one defence or transport behaviour.
L20.assessment: Explain how a kangaroo pouch and a hen's response can improve the survival of young.
L20.evidence: The pouch shelters and carries the joey. A hen may drive away a threat from her chicks.
L20.closure: Ask pupils to name the risk reduced by their chosen example.

L21.materials: Habitat cards, paper, modelling clay, defence cards
L21.induction: Show a windy cold habitat with a predator card. Ask which problems the design must solve.
L21.teach: Model turning two observed animal traits into labelled features that meet different threats.
L21.practice: Draw and construct a model with one enemy defence and one feature for the chosen extreme weather.
L21.assessment: Attach two labels and explain how each feature addresses a different challenge.
L21.evidence: For example, thicker fur helps reduce heat loss, and a hard shell protects vulnerable body parts from a predator.
L21.closure: Ask which feature would need changing for a hot habitat.

L22.materials: Models from Lesson 21, explanation cards, peer feedback slips
L22.induction: Ask pupils to match one model feature to a real animal feature.
L22.teach: Demonstrate presenting a model through claim and reason. Discuss a predator's role in a balanced habitat.
L22.practice: Present the model and respond to one peer challenge. Add a connection to a real adaptation and habitat balance.
L22.assessment: Name one real adaptation and explain how a model feature responds to a threat. Add one reason species relationships matter.
L22.evidence: For example, body covering reduces heat loss. A predator–prey link can help keep populations in balance.
L22.closure: Ask which evidence changed an explanation during the presentation.

L23.materials: Rice plant, grasshopper and frog cards, arrow strips
L23.induction: Ask which organism can make its own food.
L23.teach: Use arrows from food to feeder. Model labelling the green plant as producer and animals as consumers.
L23.practice: Arrange cards into two chains beginning with a producer and read the arrows as energy transfer.
L23.assessment: Draw rice plant, grasshopper and frog as a chain. Label producer and consumers.
L23.evidence: Rice plant → grasshopper → frog. Rice is the producer, and the animals are consumers.
L23.closure: Ask pupils to say what moves in the direction of an arrow.

L24.materials: Sun, green plant, caterpillar and bird cards, diagram paper
L24.induction: Ask why a food chain usually begins with a green plant.
L24.teach: Distinguish sunlight as energy from the plant as producer. Link light to the food made by photosynthesis.
L24.practice: Annotate one plant-based chain to show where light is used and how energy reaches two consumers.
L24.assessment: Explain the roles of sunlight and a leaf in a leaf–caterpillar–bird chain.
L24.evidence: The plant uses light energy to make food. Energy in that food passes to the caterpillar and then to the bird.
L24.closure: Ask learners to point to the first living part of the chain.

L25.materials: Rice-field organism cards, arrows, large paper
L25.induction: Show two chains that both start with rice. Ask whether the two rice cards represent different producers.
L25.teach: Model joining chains at a shared organism, preserving the direction from food to feeder.
L25.practice: Build three linked chains using rice, grasshopper, frog, rat, snake and owl. Use the supplied feeding links to identify shared nodes.
L25.assessment: Draw three connected routes with one producer and at least one shared consumer. Explain why the diagram is a food web.
L25.evidence: Example: rice → rat → owl, rice → rat → snake and rice → grasshopper → frog → snake. Rice, rat and snake each connect more than one chain.
L25.closure: Ask whether one consumer can belong to more than one chain.

L26.materials: Rice-field food web, population change cards
L26.induction: Cover the frog card and ask which other organism loses a food source.
L26.teach: Model following arrows towards an eater and back towards its prey. Label predictions as possible effects.
L26.practice: Use rice → grasshopper → frog → snake to mark one direct and one further effect of fewer frogs.
L26.assessment: Predict one effect on grasshoppers and one on snakes after the frog population drops. Explain both.
L26.evidence: Grasshoppers may increase because fewer frogs eat them. Snakes may decline if frogs are an important food source.
L26.closure: Ask why another food source could change the predicted outcome.

R03.materials: Defence cards, small food web, exit tickets
R03.induction: Ask learners to choose an enemy defence and name the threat it reduces.
R03.teach: Refresh the meaning of an arrow using one producer–consumer link.
R03.practice: Annotate a web and write a cause-and-effect statement from a change card.
R03.assessment: Justify a tortoise's shell and predict an effect of fewer insects on a bird that eats them.
R03.evidence: The shell protects soft body parts. The bird may have less food and its population could decline.
R03.closure: Ask pupils to check that their reason matches the threat or food link.

L27.induction: Display a thorny plant photograph and ask why an animal might avoid it.
L27.teach: Model feature-to-effect links using thorns and irritating hairs. Use pictures for irritants.
L27.practice: Match two plants to protective features, then annotate a sketch for each.
L27.assessment: Explain how thorns and irritating hairs discourage animals.
L27.evidence: Thorns hinder or deter feeding. Irritating hairs cause discomfort and can deter contact.
L27.closure: Ask how a feature can help a plant survive being eaten.

L28.materials: Cactus and deciduous tree photos, season cards, postcard paper
L28.induction: Ask what a plant in a dry habitat has to conserve.
L28.teach: Compare a water-storing stem and leaf loss during unsuitable seasons. Link each trait to its environmental challenge.
L28.practice: Create two postcards from different climates with drawings and feature–benefit notes.
L28.assessment: Compare how a cactus stem and seasonal leaf fall can help plants survive.
L28.evidence: A fleshy stem stores water. Shedding leaves can reduce water loss or damage in unfavourable conditions.
L28.closure: Ask which environmental clue supports each explanation.

L29.materials: Pictures of coconut, winged seed, burr and dry pod, shallow tray
L29.induction: Show a hooked fruit and ask what its hooks might attach to.
L29.teach: Model feature-to-mechanism reasoning for wind, water, animals or people, and splitting pods.
L29.practice: Sort four examples. Test a paper wing model, then explain the role of hooks, flotation or splitting.
L29.assessment: Match coconut, winged seed, burr and splitting pod to dispersal methods. Explain two placements.
L29.evidence: Water for the floating coconut, wind for the winged seed, animals or people for the burr, and explosive mechanism for the splitting pod.
L29.closure: Ask why a feature is better evidence than the colour of the fruit.

L30.materials: Unfamiliar seed photos, prediction chart, distance sketch
L30.induction: Show a light seed with fine hairs without naming it. Ask what the hairs could do.
L30.teach: Model a claim from an observable feature. Link dispersal away from the parent plant to reduced competition.
L30.practice: Compare a hairy seed and a seed with hooks. Sketch a route away from the parent for one of them.
L30.assessment: Predict the dispersal method for the hairy seed, defend it with a visible feature and describe a benefit to the plant.
L30.evidence: Wind is a reasonable prediction because hairs help the light seed stay aloft. Movement can reduce crowding near the parent.
L30.closure: Ask which feature could instead support animal dispersal.

R04.materials: Climate photo cards, seed pictures, mini-whiteboards
R04.induction: Present a cactus and a floating fruit and ask which picture concerns dispersal.
R04.teach: Review one feature-to-benefit sentence about a dry habitat.
R04.practice: Pair one habitat clue with a plant feature and one seed feature with its dispersal route.
R04.assessment: Give a dry-habitat adaptation and predict the route of a hooked fruit.
R04.evidence: A fleshy stem can store water. A hooked fruit may attach to fur or clothing and travel with animals or people.
R04.closure: Ask pupils to name the evidence used in each prediction.

L31.materials: Energy source and device cards, source–use chart
L31.induction: Show a torch and a solar garden light. Ask where each gets electrical energy.
L31.teach: Connect a dry cell, solar cell, generator and rechargeable battery to specific devices. Distinguish conversion from use.
L31.practice: Match source cards to devices and explain one way electricity is produced or supplied.
L31.assessment: Match a torch, solar garden light, bicycle lamp and cordless drill to their sources. Explain the solar match.
L31.evidence: Examples are a dry cell, solar cell, dynamo and rechargeable battery respectively. The solar cell converts light energy into electrical energy.
L31.closure: Ask which source relies on a moving wheel.

L32.materials: Dry cells, matching bulbs, low-voltage leads, circuit symbol cards
L32.induction: Show a one-path diagram and a branching diagram without labels.
L32.teach: Model tracing from one battery terminal to the other. Sketch one closed path then two branches using standard symbols.
L32.practice: Build and trace both circuits with dry cells. Sketch them and label bulb arrangement.
L32.assessment: Sketch a complete series circuit and a complete parallel circuit with two bulbs. Explain how the arrangements differ.
L32.evidence: Both sketches include a cell and two bulb symbols. Series bulbs lie on one path. Parallel bulbs sit on separate branches.
L32.closure: Ask a pupil to trace one complete route in each sketch.

L33.materials: Matched bulbs, dry cells, bulb holders, brightness record
L33.induction: Show both circuit diagrams and ask whether their bulbs will appear equally bright.
L33.teach: Set up a matched comparison with the same type and count of cells and bulbs. Model using the same observation scale.
L33.practice: Build both circuits, record their brightness and compare observations with another group.
L33.assessment: State which bulbs appear brighter with the given setup and identify two quantities kept the same.
L33.evidence: Usually the parallel bulbs look brighter with this setup. Both circuits use the same number and type of cells and identical bulbs. Report actual observations.
L33.closure: Ask which uncontrolled change would make the comparison hard to interpret.

L34.materials: Dry cells, identical rated bulbs, two low-voltage circuit boards, results grid
L34.induction: Show a second bulb being added. Ask which quantity this investigation will change.
L34.teach: Model a safe comparison with the same cell supply, changing only the number of bulbs within each arrangement.
L34.practice: Compare one and two bulbs in each circuit arrangement. Record the brightness of an individual bulb and label each trial.
L34.assessment: Identify the variable changed and state what happens when a second bulb is added in series and in parallel.
L34.evidence: The number of bulbs changes. With the same supply, a series bulb generally dims. A parallel bulb usually changes less. Record and explain any observed variation.
L34.closure: Ask why changing the cell count during this test would obscure the result.

L35.materials: Matching bulbs, one- and two-cell holders, low-voltage leads, results grid
L35.induction: Show one cell beside two matched cells. Ask what must stay unchanged to compare brightness.
L35.teach: Use components rated for the selected cell supply. Demonstrate adding a second dry cell in series with the first and leaving both bulbs in place.
L35.practice: Compare one and two supply cells in the same bulb layout. Repeat for the other layout and summarise the results.
L35.assessment: Name the variable changed, one factor held constant and the observed effect when a second supply cell is added.
L35.evidence: The cell count changes. The same bulbs and layout are kept within each comparison. Bulbs generally brighten with the added cell within their ratings.
L35.closure: Ask how this investigation differs from changing the number of bulbs.

L36.materials: Low-voltage boards with switches, circuit maps, prediction chart
L36.induction: Open one branch switch and ask pupils to predict which lamp will go out.
L36.teach: Compare a switch in the common supply path with a switch in one branch. Include a switch anywhere in a series loop.
L36.practice: Predict and test three open-switch scenarios. Mark conducting paths and verify which bulbs light.
L36.assessment: Predict the effect of opening a switch in a series loop, one parallel branch and the common supply path.
L36.evidence: Both bulbs go out in series. Only the affected branch goes out for a branch switch. Both go out when the common supply path is opened.
L36.closure: Ask pupils which switch controls all branches.

L37.materials: Fictional appliance-use cards, sample bill totals, comparison chart
L37.induction: Show identical fans used for different times. Ask which is likely to use more electrical energy.
L37.teach: Compare duration and power rating one factor at a time. Demonstrate using a fictional bill without household data.
L37.practice: Compare two appliance-use scenarios and propose a conservation step based on a factor that changed.
L37.assessment: Compare a 50 W fan used for two hours with the same fan used for six hours. Give a way to reduce its energy use.
L37.evidence: Six hours uses three times as much energy because the power is the same. Switching off the fan when the space is empty reduces running time.
L37.closure: Ask which comparison would isolate the effect of appliance power.

L38.materials: Printed hazard scenarios, picture cards, safety-rule labels
L38.induction: Display an overloaded plug illustration. Ask pupils to spot the unsafe action.
L38.teach: Work through a printed wet-hands case. Model naming the hazard, possible consequence and safe action.
L38.practice: Sort printed examples, then write safety advice for two cases. Discuss one conservation habit from Lesson 37.
L38.assessment: Explain the risk from wet hands and from a damaged cord. State what a pupil should do in each situation.
L38.evidence: Wet hands raise shock risk. A damaged lead can expose live parts. Keep hands dry, avoid the damaged appliance and tell a responsible adult.
L38.closure: Ask pupils to distinguish energy saving from an electrical safety action.

R05.induction: Show two parallel branches and point to a switch in just one branch.
R05.teach: Trace the shared supply path and one branch. Check a sample hazard response.
R05.practice: Predict whether a lamp lights and match a hazard with its safe response.
R05.assessment: Predict the effect of opening a branch switch and explain what to do on seeing a damaged plug.
R05.evidence: The affected bulb goes out and the other branch stays lit if its path remains closed. Keep away from the plug and tell an adult.
R05.closure: Ask which part of the other branch stays complete.

L39.materials: Digital probe thermometer, cool and warm water, reading cards
L39.induction: Show two water samples and ask how to establish which is warmer without touching them.
L39.teach: Model holding the probe in the water away from the container, waiting for a stable reading and recording °C.
L39.practice: Take readings of both samples with the correct technique and compare temperatures.
L39.assessment: Explain heat and temperature briefly. Record a water reading with its unit and demonstrate probe placement.
L39.evidence: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Temperature measures hotness or coldness. The reading includes °C.
L39.closure: Ask why comparing readings requires the same temperature unit.

L40.materials: Teacher-run heating setup, digital thermometer, timer, graph grid, ice
L40.induction: Show a sample ice-to-boil graph without values. Ask where the line might flatten.
L40.teach: Use a guarded teacher demonstration or data replay. Model recording at regular times and identifying phase-change plateaus.
L40.practice: Record temperatures against time from ice to heated water. Plot the data and mark the ice-melting and boiling stages.
L40.assessment: Read the freezing and boiling temperatures from the supplied graph and explain what the axes show.
L40.evidence: Pure water at standard pressure freezes near 0°C and boils near 100°C. The graph plots temperature against elapsed time. Report the observed values.
L40.closure: Ask when adding energy can change state while temperature stays nearly steady.

L41.materials: Teacher-prepared warm and cool water, digital thermometer, room thermometer, timers
L41.induction: Ask what will happen to warm and cool water left in the same room.
L41.teach: Demonstrate measuring room temperature and tracking both samples without changing container type.
L41.practice: Measure each water sample at equal time intervals. Draw arrows to show heat transfer between the samples and the surroundings.
L41.assessment: Given a room at 27°C, predict the trends for water at 40°C and at 18°C. Explain the direction of heat transfer.
L41.evidence: The warmer water loses heat and cools towards 27°C. The cooler water gains heat and warms towards 27°C.
L41.closure: Ask which reading shows the surroundings' temperature.

L42.materials: Plastic bottle, balloon, trays of warm and cool water, diagram strips
L42.induction: Show a deflated balloon on a bottle. Ask what warm air inside the bottle might do.
L42.teach: Compare the same bottle in warm then cool water under supervision. Keep the opening covered by the same balloon.
L42.practice: Observe the balloon, record each change and use sketches to explain what happens to the air volume.
L42.assessment: Explain the different balloon shapes after warming and cooling the same bottle.
L42.evidence: Warming makes the enclosed air take up more space and the balloon expand. Cooling reduces the air volume and the balloon shrinks.
L42.closure: Ask pupils to link one observation to heat gain and one to heat loss.

L43.materials: Bridge-joint and overhead-line pictures, spaced paper strips
L43.induction: Show a gap in a bridge joint and ask why builders leave it.
L43.teach: Model paper strips that meet when they expand. Compare a bridge joint with slack in an overhead line.
L43.practice: Annotate two designs with arrows or labels that show movement as temperatures change.
L43.assessment: Explain how a bridge joint gap and slack in a cable handle expansion or contraction.
L43.evidence: The gap allows a bridge material to expand without pressing hard against its neighbour. Cable slack allows for contraction in cooler weather.
L43.closure: Ask pupils what could happen if a bridge had no movement space.

R06.materials: Thermometer display cards, bridge sketch, answer slips
R06.induction: Show a temperature display and ask for its reading to the marked precision.
R06.teach: Revisit temperature units and a single expansion example.
R06.practice: Read a display and annotate the space in a bridge sketch.
R06.assessment: Read a 32°C display, then explain why a bridge joint includes a gap.
R06.evidence: The temperature is 32°C. The gap allows material to expand when heated.
R06.closure: Ask pupils to name the unit and one design feature.

L44.materials: Photos of rusted iron and clean objects, magnet, known material samples
L44.induction: Show pictures of rough brown iron and a clean metal surface. Ask what is observable.
L44.teach: Compare iron with plastic and aluminium under the same recorded conditions. Distinguish rust from other surface changes.
L44.practice: Record colour and texture for each sample and identify which confirmed iron objects developed rust.
L44.assessment: Describe two visible signs of rust and explain what material the examples identify as capable of rusting.
L44.evidence: Rust commonly forms a rough reddish-brown layer on iron or steel. Compare the observed iron sample with the other materials.
L44.closure: Ask whether every brown surface is evidence of rust.

L45.materials: Identical uncoated iron nails, labelled clear jars, water, teacher-prepared controls
L45.induction: Show three identical iron nails and ask which conditions must differ.
L45.teach: Provide air-and-water, dry-air and pre-prepared deoxygenated-water controls. Explain which factor each comparison isolates.
L45.practice: Label jars, sketch the conditions, record the initial appearance and predict which nail will rust.
L45.assessment: Name which setup contains both conditions and explain why equal nails are used.
L45.evidence: The nail exposed to air and water is expected to rust. Using identical nails controls the material and size.
L45.closure: Ask which two setups isolate the role of water.

L46.materials: Prepared jars from Lesson 45, baseline photos, recording grid
L46.induction: Show the jars and ask what has changed since the baseline.
L46.teach: Have pupils compare without opening the controls. Model distinguishing an observation from a conclusion.
L46.practice: Record signs of rust in each jar and use the two comparisons to infer which conditions are needed.
L46.assessment: Use the observations to explain the importance of both air and water in rusting.
L46.evidence: Rust in air plus water alongside little or no rust in the other conditions supports the conclusion that both oxygen from air and water are needed.
L46.closure: Ask what a leaky or wet control could do to the result.

L47.materials: Photos of painted railings and lubricated tools, prevention cards
L47.induction: Show a patch of chipped paint on iron and ask why rust may start there.
L47.teach: Compare barriers such as paint and oil with the choice of a rust-resistant material. Link protection to durability.
L47.practice: Choose prevention methods for two objects and explain why each method is suited to the object's use.
L47.assessment: Choose a method for an outdoor iron gate and an iron hinge. Explain how each method works.
L47.evidence: Paint can protect a gate and a suitable lubricant can protect a hinge. A continuous barrier reduces contact with air and water.
L47.closure: Ask why a coating has to be maintained.

R07.induction: Ask which of two nails is more likely to rust: one in dry air or one in damp air.
R07.teach: Review the condition comparison and one way to stop water reaching iron.
R07.practice: Match a protective coating to an object and write a reason.
R07.assessment: Name both requirements for rusting and explain how painting a clean iron gate helps.
R07.evidence: Iron needs water and oxygen to rust. Paint forms a barrier that reduces contact with both.
R07.closure: Ask why bare scratches are more vulnerable.

L48.materials: Stone, water, inflated bag, material picture cards
L48.induction: Show a sealed bag of air. Ask whether the air counts as matter.
L48.teach: Compare familiar solid, liquid and gas examples. Use a filled bag to show that gas takes up space.
L48.practice: Sort material cards and justify two placements using properties pupils can see or test.
L48.assessment: Sort ice, water and air. Give one reason that a bag of air contains matter.
L48.evidence: Ice is solid, water is liquid in the example, and air is gas. Air takes up space in the bag.
L48.closure: Ask which material changes its outline when poured.

L49.materials: Block, water, two measuring cups, sealed needle-free syringes
L49.induction: Show a block and equal measured liquid in differently shaped cups.
L49.teach: Model observing shape and volume separately. Compare equal-volume samples of air and water gently in sealed syringes.
L49.practice: Record which materials keep shape, keep volume or compress, and compare the observations.
L49.assessment: Complete the three-state comparison and explain what the syringe demonstrates.
L49.evidence: Solids keep shape and volume. Liquids keep volume and take the container's shape. Gases spread to fill space and compress more readily.
L49.closure: Ask whether pouring the liquid changes its measured volume.

L50.materials: Ice, liquid water, cold lid, water vapour diagram
L50.induction: Show an ice cube and a wet surface and ask what substance they share.
L50.teach: Link ice and liquid water to the invisible gas state. Distinguish visible mist droplets from water vapour.
L50.practice: Make a three-panel record. Use droplets forming on the cold lid as indirect evidence of water vapour condensing.
L50.assessment: Name the three states of water and explain where the droplets on the lid came from.
L50.evidence: Ice is solid, liquid water flows and water vapour is an invisible gas. Cooling vapour at the lid forms liquid droplets.
L50.closure: Ask why a visible white mist is not the gas state itself.

L51.materials: Ice, cold lid, cup, teacher-prepared observation sequence, state cards
L51.induction: Show droplets on a cold lid and ask which state change might explain them.
L51.teach: Demonstrate melting and condensation, then show prepared examples of freezing, evaporation and teacher-observed boiling.
L51.practice: Arrange evidence cards around a state diagram and label all five processes.
L51.assessment: Label solid to liquid, liquid to solid, liquid to gas and gas to liquid. Name both routes from liquid to gas.
L51.evidence: Melting, freezing, evaporation or boiling, and condensation respectively. Boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling point.
L51.closure: Ask which process can occur from a liquid surface below its boiling point.

L52.materials: Ice, sealed cooling samples, state cards, heat-transfer arrows
L52.induction: Ask whether drops forming on a chilled surface gained or lost heat.
L52.teach: Model energy arrows for melting, freezing, evaporation, boiling and condensation. Use supervised demonstrations or prepared evidence.
L52.practice: Compare before-and-after evidence and attach heat arrows to each state change.
L52.assessment: Classify all five processes as heat gain or loss and explain one with observed evidence.
L52.evidence: Melting, evaporation and boiling involve heat gain. Freezing and condensation involve heat loss. For example, cooling vapour makes liquid droplets.
L52.closure: Ask which reverse process releases energy.

L53.materials: Clear container, warm water, cold lid, cloud-cycle sketch
L53.induction: Ask how droplets can appear above the water level inside a covered container.
L53.teach: Model evaporation from warm water and condensation on the cold lid. Link growing drops to precipitation.
L53.practice: Observe the covered model and label evaporation, cooling, condensation and falling droplets.
L53.assessment: Explain how a cloud forms from water vapour and why some droplets later fall as rain.
L53.evidence: Air containing vapour cools and vapour condenses into cloud droplets. Drops grow and fall when large enough.
L53.closure: Ask where the lid model differs from a real cloud.

R08.materials: Water state cards, cloud sequence diagram, blank arrows
R08.induction: Ask pupils to choose the process that makes liquid droplets from water vapour.
R08.teach: Review one state change and organise one cloud-model picture.
R08.practice: Match water processes to state arrows and put the rain sequence in order.
R08.assessment: Label liquid to gas at the surface and gas to liquid. Explain one step from cloud droplets to rain.
R08.evidence: Evaporation makes vapour and condensation makes liquid droplets. Drops can grow and then fall as rain.
R08.closure: Ask which step happens when vapour cools.

L54.materials: Fixed lamp, marked Moon ball, Earth marker, timing cards
L54.induction: Shine light on a Moon ball and ask what makes one half appear bright.
L54.teach: Model reflection, then an orbit while the marked face stays oriented towards Earth. Show anticlockwise movement viewed from above the north side and about 27 days per turn or orbit.
L54.practice: Use the model to show one rotation per revolution. Record direction and explain which light source is required.
L54.assessment: Demonstrate both motions, state their approximate durations and explain why the Moon is visible.
L54.evidence: The Moon reflects sunlight. Viewed from the north side, it rotates and orbits anticlockwise, taking about 27 days for each relative to the stars.
L54.closure: Ask which movement is around Earth's position and which is about the Moon's own axis.

L55.materials: Moon-phase cards, lamp and ball, sample lunar calendar
L55.induction: Show first and last quarter drawings and ask which appears before full Moon.
L55.teach: Model the visible lit part from Earth's position and distinguish the approximately 29.5-day phase cycle from the orbit period relative to stars.
L55.practice: Arrange the phases from new Moon to the next new Moon. Mark four positions on a circular calendar.
L55.assessment: Order new Moon, first quarter, full Moon and last quarter. Explain how the sequence marks a lunar month.
L55.evidence: New → first quarter → full → last quarter → new. The changing visible lit portion repeats in about 29.5 days.
L55.closure: Ask why Earth's shadow does not explain the ordinary phases.

L56.materials: Star-pattern cards, named reference sheet, direction arrows
L56.induction: Reveal a cross pattern and ask how it differs from the Big Dipper pattern.
L56.teach: Compare Orion, Big Dipper, Southern Cross and Scorpion. Model one direction or seasonal use without implying that patterns are always visible.
L56.practice: Match outlines to names and annotate one use for a selected pattern.
L56.assessment: Identify two given patterns and give one use of a named constellation.
L56.evidence: For example, the Southern Cross can help find south. A pattern's seasonal appearance can also be used as a calendar clue.
L56.closure: Ask how repeated observation helps recognise a pattern.

L57.materials: Star-chart extracts, stickers, dark card, labels
L57.induction: Show two similar outlines and ask which feature helps distinguish them.
L57.teach: Model placing stars relative to each other and connecting only enough lines to recognise the pattern.
L57.practice: Make and label a star map for Orion, Southern Cross, Big Dipper or Scorpion. Explain one use or identifying feature.
L57.assessment: Present a correctly labelled pattern and support the identification with one feature and a use.
L57.evidence: For example, Orion has three prominent belt stars in a line. Its appearance can be used as a seasonal reference.
L57.closure: Ask whether rotating the paper changes the relative positions of its stars.

R09.materials: Moon-phase cards, constellation diagrams, response slips
R09.induction: Show full Moon and half-visible Moon cards. Ask which can follow a new Moon first.
R09.teach: Review a four-phase cycle and compare two named star patterns.
R09.practice: Sequence phase cards and annotate one constellation with its use.
R09.assessment: Put the four main phases in order and state one use of the Southern Cross.
R09.evidence: New, first quarter, full, last quarter, then new again. The Southern Cross helps locate south.
R09.closure: Ask which phase precedes the full Moon in the sequence.

L58.materials: Blunt school scissors, tool photos, simple-machine cards
L58.induction: Show school scissors and ask what pressing the handles does at the blades.
L58.teach: Model identifying lever arms and the wedge shape of the blade edges on a real pair of scissors.
L58.practice: Observe the tool and annotate the pivot, handles and cutting edges. Link each component to cutting paper.
L58.assessment: Label the two simple machines in scissors and state what each contributes.
L58.evidence: The handles and blades pivot as levers. Blade edges act as wedges that separate the material.
L58.closure: Ask why the pivot helps move both blades.

L59.materials: Blunt scissors, hand-crank pencil sharpener, action cards
L59.induction: Ask what each tool needs to do before paper or pencil material can be cut.
L59.teach: Compare pressing a lever with turning a crank, then trace how each movement drives the cutting part.
L59.practice: Make a two-column comparison: input movement, mechanism and useful output for each tool.
L59.assessment: Explain why scissors combine levers and wedges, and how a crank and cutting edge cooperate in the sharpener.
L59.evidence: The levers move and press the scissors' wedges through paper. The sharpener crank turns the mechanism so a cutting edge removes material.
L59.closure: Ask which parts would still move if the cutting edge were removed.

L60.materials: Design cards, paper, recycled cardboard, sample labels
L60.induction: Show a tool that breaks when a handle wears out. Ask what makes it easier to maintain.
L60.teach: Model a hand-operated tool concept. Link a machine feature to the task and a sustainable feature to service life or repair.
L60.practice: Propose a tool for a daily problem, label its simple machines and explain one design choice for maintenance, material or safety.
L60.assessment: Sketch the tool. Explain how two simple machines help it work and justify one sustainable feature.
L60.evidence: For example, lever handles and wedge edges help a reusable paper cutter work. A replaceable worn part can extend the service life.
L60.closure: Ask which single feature would reduce the need to replace the whole tool.

R10.induction: Show the handle, pivot and blade of a tool without labels.
R10.teach: Review how the blade edge and handle movement work together.
R10.practice: Complete the labels and explain what each simple machine contributes.
R10.assessment: Label the lever and wedge in scissors and explain each function.
R10.evidence: The lever pivots to press the blades and the wedge-shaped edges separate the paper.
R10.closure: Ask what function would be lost if the pivot could not move.
